01-the-liquidity-lie.delivers: S — all four objectives are met on the page: sweep identification, stop placement, the reclaim entry, and Janus Atlas.
01-the-liquidity-lie.easy_to_follow: S — was A. 'Reclaim' is the word the lesson turns on and it was used in the case study nine screens before Part 2 defined it; the definition now sits above its first use.
01-the-liquidity-lie.easy_to_get: S — the claim lands in the second paragraph: obvious levels are hunting grounds, and if you cannot see the sweep you are the liquidity. Title, hook and Part 1 all point the same way.
01-the-liquidity-lie.evidence: A — was C. The composite's 68.0% win rate and +$31,400 profit box is gone, the $16,600 counterfactual now states the two measured figures (stop depth, average rally) and what they imply rather than a sum he earned, and the invented 'top 5% of serious traders' line is out. Four sweep patterns are concrete and distinguishable
Every objective is delivered
01-the-liquidity-lie.worth_the_time: A — teaches a real mechanism (stop clustering, sweep, reclaim) and lands four named sweep patterns and four mistakes with fixes. Correct depth for lesson one.

02-volume-doesnt-lie.delivers: S — all four objectives land: delta, the two patterns, the three profile components, Plutus Flow.
02-volume-doesnt-lie.easy_to_follow: S — every load-bearing term is defined at the point of need: delta up front, absorption/exhaustion previewed before Derek, CVD when divergence arrives, then POC/HVN/LVN one at a time. Nothing requires scrolling back.
02-volume-doesnt-lie.easy_to_get: S — opens on a concrete puzzle (two identical volume bars, opposite outcomes) and answers it immediately: volume is quantity, delta is quality. A 'Quick Definition: what is delta' block sits BEFORE the case study, which is the right order and rare.
02-volume-doesnt-lie.evidence: A — was D. The '🔄 Recovery' box asserting a 74% win rate and +$65,000 is gone; the New Rules list it wrapped, which is the actual payload, stayed. 'Print money' (which five of eleven locales had already quietly softened) and 'every single one of 47 trades' are both out.
strengths: Definition-before-demonstration, done properly
The absorption/exhaustion table is the clearest thing in the beginner tier
Each profile component gets definition, why it matters, how to trade it
02-volume-doesnt-lie.worth_the_time: A — was B. The delta thresholds were absolute (+3,000 / -5,000) with no instrument named, so they were unusable at best and misleading at worst. They now read against the instrument's own typical bar, which is the only way delta means anything.

03-price-action-is-dead.delivers: S — all five objectives are met, including the Volume Oracle regime tie-in that lessons often promise and skip.
03-price-action-is-dead.easy_to_follow: S — was B. 'Cumulative delta' is the case study's entire diagnosis and was not defined until Part 2; it is now defined immediately before the diagnosis relies on it.
03-price-action-is-dead.easy_to_get: A — 'the candle shows WHERE price traded, order flow shows HOW it got there' is a clean thesis, stated in the first three sentences and never lost.
03-price-action-is-dead.evidence: A — was C. The footprint worked example now reconciles: bottom band +4,600, top band -7,970, net -3,370, and the arithmetic checks. It previously claimed the bottom band was +2,210, which was one row's delta from near the TOP with its sign flipped — an error the lesson's own ideal reader would have caught. The tape keeps its second-resolution prints, because a beginner learning to read prints needs to see prints, and gains the word 'illustrative'.
strengths: Thesis is stated in three sentences and holds for the whole lesson
Iceberg mechanics explained from the institution's problem, not as a definition
The three-layer framework gives the reader a repeatable check
weaknesses: The brief HVN/LVN restatement overlaps lesson 2 — kept deliberately: it is short, framed for order flow rather than volume profile, and the corpus-wide check found no shared passage between the two lessons
03-price-action-is-dead.worth_the_time: A — tape reading, footprint, imbalances, iceberg detection and a three-layer confirmation framework. Arguably too deep for the beginner tier: this is the third lesson and it is teaching iceberg detection.

04-repaint-problem.easy_to_follow: S — definition, cost, case, what deterministic means, then the audit framework. Nothing is used before it is explained.
04-repaint-problem.easy_to_get: S — the best opening in the tier. A 9:38 AM scenario, then the definition in one sentence: a signal that moves or vanishes after its bar has closed. Then why that costs you the whole edge.
04-repaint-problem.evidence: A — named third-party products replaced with the indicator CATEGORY each stood for, which is what the lesson teaches anyway and what the brand's own compliance guide requires ('avoid making claims about competitor products'). The red-flag rule is corrected too: a low win rate was never the tell, a curve with no pain in it is.
fixed: Named products -> categories, with a line explaining why no indicator is accused on anyone's word
Walk-forward objective replaced with the four-way audit the lesson teaches
'60-90% of indicators repaint' removed from objectives, meta description and takeaways

Either add the walk-forward section or remove it from the objectives
Drop the 60-90% figure or source it
Correct the win-rate claim: expectancy, not win rate, is what makes an edge

strengths: Definition-first opening that a reader can restate immediately
Bar Replay walkthrough is genuinely usable
Pine Script red flags with actual code, not hand-waving

Objective promises walk-forward testing that the lesson never covers

04-repaint-problem.worth_the_time: S — the most actionable lesson so far: an audit checklist, a step-by-step Bar Replay walkthrough, and Pine Script red flags with real code. This is hard to find elsewhere and it is correct.

05-rsi-extremes.delivers: S — all four objectives are met.
05-rsi-extremes.easy_to_follow: A — Part 3 opens with an explicit roadmap ('There are three, and the rest of this lesson is each of them in turn'), which is the best signposting in the tier. Cosmetic: the Part 3 heading runs into the next one with no space.
05-rsi-extremes.easy_to_get: S — gives the correct, deflationary definition of RSI ('recent up-moves have been much larger than recent down-moves, nothing more') and then the thesis: the same reading means three different things in three regimes.
05-rsi-extremes.evidence: A — was C, and the contradiction is resolved. Part 2 warns that any precise figure about algorithm behaviour, 'including one you read here', is a guess dressed up as data; two screens earlier the lesson quoted a win rate to one decimal off 55 trades. That now reads '20 of them winners' — same fact, checkable, no false precision. The $31,800 counterfactual is gone; the measured finding beside it (average rally after her exits) carries the point.
strengths: The RSI definition is correct and deflationary, which is rare
Explicit roadmap sentence before the three scenarios
Part 2's honesty note about unknowable institutional parameters
05-rsi-extremes.worth_the_time: S — goes well past overbought/oversold: regime-dependence, four divergence types, multi-timeframe alignment, and volume/delta confluence.

06-moving-averages.delivers: A — was C, and this was the real defect. One objective claimed crossovers are lagging with '60-80% of move already done' while the body says 20-30% in eleven places, including the arithmetic that derives it and the quiz answer that tests it. Another promised the reader would apply the Pilot Line, which the lesson never explained. A third said 'trade pullbacks TO moving averages' under a title reading Stop Buying the Touch. All three now match the lesson underneath them.
06-moving-averages.easy_to_follow: A — was B. Builds well: myth, then what MAs actually show, then why algos react anyway, then the Golden Cross arithmetic, then the event framework. The one break was 'Pilot Line', a proper noun doing load-bearing work in three of the five event definitions with nothing behind it anywhere on the page; it is now defined before Part 4 leans on it, and the definition earns its place by saying how this line differs from the 50 EMA the lesson has just spent five sections demolishing.
06-moving-averages.easy_to_get: S — the hook is a timestamped 40 seconds (10:18 touch, 10:22 through it, stop gone) and then the claim in plain words: a 50-period EMA is the average of the last fifty closes, no order sits at that number. Title, hook and Part 1 all argue the same thing.
06-moving-averages.evidence: A — was B. The composite's win rate went to counts (16 of 45). The bare '60-70%' algo share now says it is an industry estimate that moves with venue and instrument — which this lesson, three sections from its own model caveat, had no excuse not to do. And 'acting on TD alone = getting faked out 50% of the time' is replaced by what TD actually claims: selling looks exhausted, which is not the same as the reversal having started.
strengths: The Golden Cross lag is derived from the arithmetic, not asserted
Its working-figures caveat is the model the rest of the corpus should follow
The retail-belief vs reality split is concrete and hard to misread
Explains why MAs sometimes 'work' (clustered algo behaviour) without conceding they are support
weaknesses: Four product names (Janus Atlas, Plutus Flow, Volume Oracle, Pentarch) arrive in the Step 3 checklist with one-line glosses — acceptable at lesson 6 because each is cross-linked, but it is the densest product moment in the beginner tier
06-moving-averages.worth_the_time: S — the Golden Cross section is the best thing in the beginner tier. It does not assert the lag, it derives it: a 50-bar average has to cross a 200-bar average, so price must have risen for weeks first. And its stat box carries the caveat the rest of the corpus should copy — 'these are working figures, not a published study … check the lag yourself on the instrument you actually trade.'

07-revenge-trading.delivers: S — four objectives, four delivered, nothing major taught that no objective mentions.
07-revenge-trading.easy_to_follow: S — the strongest build in the tier. Cascade (loss aversion → cortisol → prefrontal shutdown → the trade), then the three tilts, then the case, then the four circuit breakers, then daily prep. Every term is defined before it is relied on, and the case study is placed after the mechanism it illustrates rather than before it.
07-revenge-trading.easy_to_get: S — opens in second person on the thing itself ('you're opening another trade. Bigger size this time. No setup. No plan. Just rage.') and then names the claim in two sentences: this isn't a discipline problem, it's a neuroscience problem. Nothing in the lesson pulls against that.
07-revenge-trading.evidence: S — the best-evidenced lesson so far, and the only correction needed was one rounding slip. Loss aversion is attributed to Kahneman and Tversky by name, given as roughly 2:1, and explicitly hedged: 'the exact ratio varies by person and context, but the asymmetry itself is well established.' The case study's arithmetic reconciles at every step — the running P&L chain (340, 1,580, 6,260, 15,180, 23,400), the 69x multiplier, the $17,140 the three-strike rule saves, the $16,400 the loss limit saves, and the 3x size costing $1,240 where 1x costs about $410. The cooldown argument is checked against the case study's own timestamps: 26, 29 and 29 minutes between trades, so three of the four fall inside a thirty-minute cooldown. Only the drawdown was wrong — $23,400 on $350,000 is 6.7%, not 6.8% — and it is now right.
strengths: The circuit breakers are distinguished by what each limits, not just listed
Every one carries a 'without willpower' version, which the neuroscience section makes necessary
The cooldown claim is tested against the case study's own timestamps rather than asserted
Loss aversion is named, sourced and hedged in one sentence
Winner's tilt and boredom tilt are genuinely useful additions — most treatments only cover revenge
weaknesses: 'Marcus entered all 4 revenge trades at emotional state 2-3' appears only in the Quick Wins, as a self-report the case study never recorded — harmless, but it is the one number in the lesson that is not derived from something stated earlier
07-revenge-trading.worth_the_time: S — the four circuit breakers are separated by what each one actually limits, which is the non-obvious part: the strike count caps how many times you can be wrong, the loss limit caps what each of those times may cost, the cooldown caps how fast they arrive, and the size lock caps the acceleration. Most treatments of this topic list the same four rules without ever saying why you need more than one. Each also carries a 'making it work without willpower' step, which follows directly from the neuroscience the lesson opened with.

08-confirmation-bias.easy_to_follow: A — builds well: what it is, three ways it shows up, the echo chamber that amplifies it, falsification as the counter, the red-team drill, then systems, then the case study last. CVD and HTF both arrive un-expanded in the Real Example, but both were introduced earlier in the tier (lessons 2-3 and 6), so this is a reminder problem rather than a forward reference.
08-confirmation-bias.easy_to_get: S — the opening is the cleanest statement of the idea in the corpus: you and your friend look at the same candle and see opposite things. The claim lands in four sentences and the lesson never drifts from it.
08-confirmation-bias.evidence: A — was C, and this was the whole of the gap. The worst of it was the BTC $45k head-to-head, where the retail trader is stopped for -$500 and the professional skips the trade AND re-enters lower AND makes +$1,300. The professional wins twice, by construction, in an example built to let him. What that teaches is that falsification pays; the honest claim is narrower and more useful, and the lesson makes it elsewhere ('the trades you DON'T take will save your account'). The outcome now says so directly: you are not buying a better hit rate, you are buying the ability to state before entry what would make you wrong. Also fixed: '10x worse' (a multiplier with nothing behind it), a feed that is '100% bullish, 0% bearish' (hyperbole printed as a finding, in a lesson about mistaking certainty for evidence), and Alex's -$2,200 counterfactual, which reconciles with none of the tranches the case study describes — on equal shares the loss at $285 is about $1,100, on equal dollars about $1,000.
strengths: The opening states the idea in four sentences with no jargon
The invalidation step in the red-team checklist is the part most treatments omit
Trap #1 catches hindsight bias specifically, which is usually conflated with confirmation bias
Systems-over-willpower is carried forward correctly from lesson 07
weaknesses: The echo-chamber part is a full section on a widely known point, and is the least dense stretch of the lesson
'30% win rate' in the selective-memory example is illustrative and flagged as such, but it is still a number doing rhetorical work
08-confirmation-bias.worth_the_time: A — the red-team checklist is genuinely actionable and the invalidation step ('at what price is the bull case DEAD?') is the part most treatments leave out. The three objectivity systems are practical. The echo-chamber section is the weakest: correct, but the point is widely known and the lesson spends a full part on it.

09-position-sizing.delivers: S — four objectives, four delivered, including the one most sizing lessons skip: when the right size is zero.
09-position-sizing.easy_to_follow: A — expectancy, then fixed fractional, then ATR, then portfolio heat, then the checklist, then the mistakes. Each part needs only what came before.
09-position-sizing.easy_to_get: S — 'You have a 60% win rate. Your friend has 40%. Who makes more money?' is the whole lesson in three sentences, and the expectancy table right after it settles the question with arithmetic rather than assertion.
09-position-sizing.evidence: A — was B, and the problem was a contradiction rather than a fabrication. Part 2 stated the rule as 'never risk more than 1% on a single trade' and Parts 3, 5 and 6 then sized A-grade setups at 2%, with a quiz asking why flat 1% is 'amateur hour'. In a risk lesson aimed at beginners that is the sentence most likely to be acted on, and the page said both things. It now reads '1% on a single trade, and never more than 2% however good the setup looks', and the quiz asks what flat sizing gives up rather than calling it amateur. The explanation now says plainly that until your own journal shows your grades separate your outcomes, flat 1% is the correct size and not a beginner's mistake — which is what the lesson's own practice exercise already concedes. Also: 'makes almost 3x per trade' compared +$140 with -$50, which is not a multiple of anything; 'even A-grade setups fail 30-40% of the time' was an invented rate; and Mike's counterfactual quietly dropped the trade he won, so it is now stated with the winner included.
strengths: Expectancy is derived with two worked traders, not asserted
Mike's cascade is arithmetically exact at every step, including the 10%-of-current-balance compounding
The drawdown-recovery table (10 needs 11.1, 20 needs 25, 50 needs 100) is correct and rarely shown
The practice exercise refuses to predict the reader's result and says why
weaknesses: Grading setups A/B/C is introduced as though the reader can already do it reliably; the exercise later admits they probably cannot
09-position-sizing.worth_the_time: A — the drawdown-recovery arithmetic in Mistake #5 is the part most beginners have never seen stated (a 20% loss needs a 25% gain, a 50% loss needs 100%), and every figure in it checks out.

10-stop-losses.delivers: A — four objectives, four delivered. Breakeven-at-1R and never-widening are both covered.
10-stop-losses.easy_to_follow: A — percentage stops fail, then ATR for how far, then structure for where, then the 2R rule, then a six-step placement procedure. 'ATR tells you HOW FAR. Structure tells you WHERE' is the cleanest sentence in the tier.
10-stop-losses.easy_to_get: S — the hook is the exact experience the lesson is about: stopped at 2%, then a 10% rally without you. The claim ('the market has no idea what 2% of your account is') is the thesis and never wavers.
10-stop-losses.evidence: A — was C, and this lesson needed the most repair of any so far. Three things. First, a quiz was grammatically broken: 'You observe at $100 ... Where often your stop be?' and 'Stop placement often be structure-based' — what an automated should-to-often hedging pass leaves behind when it hits a modal verb. This is the only lesson in the corpus where that pass broke the grammar, and it broke the question a beginner is asked to answer. Second, the 2R quiz illustrated a 40% win rate with '4 losses + 6 wins', which is 60%, and claimed you need '60%+ accuracy' below 2R when at 1:1 you need 50%. Third and largest, a six-method comparison table reported stop-out rate, false-stop rate, average loss, win rate and expectancy 'based on Kevin's 8-month testing' — but the case study says Kevin traded three methods and settled on a fourth. The 1.5x and 3.0x rows were measurements of an experiment that never happened, under a heading reading 'What The Data Shows'. The five invented columns are gone; the methods and their use cases remain, because Part 2 already derives that comparison honestly. The recovery phase's +91% and its supporting statistics went too.
strengths: 'ATR tells you HOW FAR. Structure tells you WHERE' organises the whole lesson in eight words
The break-even hit rate is derived per ratio rather than asserted
Step 4 makes stop distance an input and size an output, and says so explicitly
Sarah's stop-moving sequence is short, concrete and arithmetically exact
weaknesses: Kevin's case study is long — 622 words — and its three phases restate a point Part 1 has already made
The remaining phase statistics for the two failed methods are still composite figures; they are kept because a disaster record illustrates a mistake rather than claiming a return
10-stop-losses.worth_the_time: S — the 2R section derives the break-even hit rate at each ratio (1:1 needs 50%, 2:1 needs 33%, 3:1 needs 25%) instead of asserting a rule, and the six-step procedure makes stop distance an input and position size an output, which is the actual inversion most traders never make.

11-timeframe-illusion.easy_to_follow: A — addiction trap, then the mechanism, then the alignment framework, then timeframe by account size, then costs, then the matrix. HTF/MTF/LTF are expanded on first use.
11-timeframe-illusion.easy_to_get: S — the best hook in the tier. Same instrument, same moment: the 5-minute chart shows a clean breakout, the daily shows a lower high three days into a downtrend. 'Both charts are right ... on a 5-minute chart you are looking at a keyhole.' Then the structural claim: 390 bars against 1 is not 390 times the insight, it is 390 times as many moments in which you can talk yourself into a trade.
11-timeframe-illusion.evidence: A — was D, and this was the sharpest self-contradiction in the corpus. Part 1 contains the best caveat anywhere in these 82 lessons: 'no public dataset cleanly measures retail returns by timeframe, so treat any precise figure quoted for this — here or anywhere else — as invented.' The matrix in Part 5 repeats it. Part 2 was then a precise figure for retail returns by timeframe: Jessica turning -$18,300 a year into +$46,116, a 145.5% annual return, off a timeframe change; Tom's recovery quantified to the dollar; three-year projections; and a burnout table giving the percentage who quit. The Key Takeaways headed the pair 'Real examples prove the pattern' and added 'Pattern repeats across thousands of traders' — twice — which is exactly the population claim the lesson had already said nobody can make. All of it is gone. The behavioural changes stay, because they are what a reader can copy and they are not claims about what the method earns: 3,355 trades against 52, 1,560 hours against 120, and a commission bill that fell with the count.
strengths: The Part 1 caveat is the model the whole corpus should follow, and it is now the only kind of claim the lesson makes
The keyhole image does more work than any statistic could
'Higher timeframes do not have a better win rate. They give you fewer chances to be wrong, and charge you less each time you are' is the honest version of the thesis
Smaller-account-means-higher-timeframe is counterintuitive, correct, and derived from cost as a share of capital
weaknesses: Two composite traders still carry the emotional weight of Parts 1 and 2; they now illustrate rather than prove, but the lesson would lose nothing by being shorter
11-timeframe-illusion.worth_the_time: S — the argument is structural rather than statistical and says so: more bars means more decisions, your error rate per decision does not fall because there are more of them, every decision pays a spread, and the cost scales with frequency while your edge does not. That survives being asked where it came from.
